content: Vin Mariani, also known as Mariani's wine, was a tonic developed around 1863 by Angelo Mariani, a French chemist. Mariani became fascinated with the coca plant and its potential economic value after reading a scientific paper by Paolo Mantegazza that detailed the physiological effects of coca. The tonic was created by infusing Bordeaux wine with coca leaves. The ethanol in the wine acted as a solvent, extracting cocaine from the coca leaves and thereby enhancing the drink's pharmacological effects. The original formulation of Vin Mariani contained approximately 6 milligrams of cocaine per fluid ounce of wine. However, the version of the tonic intended for export contained a slightly higher concentration of cocaine, at 7.2 milligrams per ounce, to remain competitive with similar coca-based beverages in the United States, which often had higher cocaine content. Vin Mariani served as the inspiration for John S. Pemberton's creation of a similar product in 1884, known as Pemberton's French Wine Coca. However, when Atlanta and Fulton County enacted Prohibition laws in 1885, Pemberton reformulated his product into a non-alcoholic, carbonated beverage, which he named Coca-Cola. This new drink retained coca leaves as a source of its stimulant properties and incorporated kola nuts, which provided caffeine. As a result, Angelo Mariani is sometimes referred to as the grandfather of Coca-Cola. When cocaine is consumed alone, it metabolizes into two primary active compounds: benzoylecgonine and ecgonine methyl ester. However, when cocaine is combined with alcohol, as in the case of Vin Mariani, a third compound, cocaethylene, is formed. Cocaethylene is a psychoactive substance that is more euphoric than cocaine alone but also significantly more toxic to the cardiovascular system. Vin Mariani achieved widespread popularity during its time, attracting a diverse and prestigious clientele, including royalty and religious leaders. Queen Victoria of Great Britain and Ireland was known to consume the tonic. Pope Leo XIII and his successor, Pope Saint Pius X, were also enthusiasts of Vin Mariani. Pope Leo XIII even awarded the wine a Vatican gold medal and appeared in promotional materials endorsing the product. In recent years, a group of UK investors under the name Mariani Amalgamated Ltd. has revived the production of Vin Mariani.
